notes.meaning: Reuben was the oldest son of Jacob, but he lost his rights as the firstborn because of a shameful sin against his father. A birthright normally gave the oldest son a double portion of land and family leadership. Because of Reuben's sin, that double share was transferred to the two sons of Joseph.

The tribe of Judah grew into the strongest tribe and received the royal blessing of leadership. King David and eventually the Messiah came from Judah, even though the double portion of land went to Joseph. For this reason, the family registers list Judah in the place of highest honor.

Reuben's four sons were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These sons became the main family branches that made up the tribe of Reuben. Even though Reuben lost his birthright, his family was still counted among God's people.

This list traces seven generations from Joel down to Beerah. Beerah was a leading chief among the Reubenites when King Tiglath-pileser of Assyria marched in and carried the eastern tribes away as captives. His name marks the end of their independent rule in their homeland.

Beerah's relatives and clan leaders were recorded in the official family rolls. Leaders such as Jeiel, Zechariah, and Bela settled across Reubenite territory east of the Jordan River, reaching towns like Aroer, Nebo, and Baal-meon.

Bela's family expanded their pasturelands eastward toward the wilderness near the Euphrates River. They pushed outward because their livestock had increased so greatly in the land of Gilead. God provided more grazing ground as His people grew in number.

During the reign of King Saul, the Reubenites went to war against the Hagrites, an Arab desert people living in tents. Reuben defeated them and moved into their camps throughout the eastern region of Gilead.

The tribe of Gad settled right next to Reuben, making their home in the northern region of Bashan all the way to Salecah. Joel served as their principal chief, with Shapham next in command, alongside Jaanai and Shaphat.
Seven other family heads are named as kinsmen of the Gadite chiefs. Their ancestry is traced upward through several generations to Buz, with Ahi acting as the chief over these households.
These Gadite families lived throughout Gilead, the towns of Bashan, and across the rich pasturelands of Sharon. This fertile country gave them plenty of open space to graze their herds.

The family records of Gad were formally written down during the reigns of King Jotham of Judah and King Jeroboam II of Israel. These lists proved their genuine Israelite heritage just before Assyria invaded. God preserved an inventory of His people to show they were not forgotten forever.
The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh assembled an army of 44,760 brave soldiers. These men were well trained for war and skilled with swords, shields, and bows.
These eastern tribes fought against the Hagrites and other Ishmaelite clans named Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. These nomadic desert neighbors had frequently troubled the borders of Israel.

During the heat of battle, the Israelite soldiers called out to God for help. God answered their prayers and handed the enemies over to them because they put their trust in Him rather than their own weapons. Trusting prayer wins God's help in our hardest struggles.

The Israelites seized vast amounts of property from the Hagrites, including thousands of camels, sheep, and donkeys. They also took one hundred thousand captives. This enormous haul of livestock showed how completely the desert tribes were defeated.

A vast number of enemy soldiers fell in battle because God Himself directed the fight. The eastern tribes then moved into that territory and lived there safely until the Assyrian exile came. When God fights for His people, their victory is secure.

The people of the half-tribe of Manasseh multiplied greatly and spread northward from Bashan toward Mount Hermon. Seven prominent leaders are listed, known as famous men and mighty warriors who governed their expanding households.

In spite of God's great goodness, these eastern tribes turned away from the God of their fathers. They began worshipping the false gods of the pagan peoples whom God had previously destroyed before them. Their unfaithfulness broke the special bond they had with the Lord.

Because they turned to idols, God stirred up the kings of Assyria, Pul and Tiglath-pileser, to conquer the eastern tribes. The Assyrian armies carried Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh into foreign exile in lands like Halah and Habor. Abandoning God left them without His protection against their enemies.
